Burdensome
bûr´d'n-sŭm
adj. (heavy to carry; a weight upon others; rendering Greek katanarkao and baros, Hebrew ma'amasah)
Burden + some. Paul's word is a dead weight that numbs what it lies on; Zechariah's is a stone that ruptures the men who lift it.

Biblical Definition

Paul to Corinth: “what is it wherein ye were inferior to other churches, except it be that I myself was not burdensome to you? forgive me this wrong” (2Co 12:13); “the third time I am ready to come to you; and I will not be burdensome to you: for I seek not yours, but you” (2Co 12:14). To Thessalonica: “Nor of men sought we glory… when we might have been burdensome, as the apostles of Christ” (1Th 2:6). Zechariah: “in that day will I make Jerusalem a burdensome stone for all people: all that burden themselves with it shall be cut in pieces” (Zec 12:3).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines burdensome as grievous to be borne; causing uneasiness or fatigue; oppressive.

expand to see more

BURDENSOME, a. Grievous to be borne; causing uneasiness or fatigue; oppressive.

Key Scripture

2Co 12:14 — "Behold, the third time I am ready to come to you; and I will not be burdensome to you: for I seek not yours, but you: for the children ought not to lay up for the parents, but the parents for the children."

2Co 12:13 — "For what is it wherein ye were inferior to other churches, except it be that I myself was not burdensome to you? forgive me this wrong."

1Th 2:6 — "Nor of men sought we glory, neither of you, nor yet of others, when we might have been burdensome, as the apostles of Christ."

Zec 12:3 — "And in that day will I make Jerusalem a burdensome stone for all people: all that burden themselves with it shall be cut in pieces, though all the people of the earth be gathered together against it."

Modern Corruption

Ministers seek yours and not you, and Paul's refusal to be burdensome was the proof that he sought the Corinthians and not their purse.

expand to see more

“I seek not yours, but you” is the sentence under Paul's whole practice at Corinth. He had the right to be burdensome as an apostle and set it aside, and when the Corinthians took his refusal as proof that he did not love them he asked their pardon for the wrong with an irony they could not miss. The minister who seeks the congregation's goods and calls it faith-giving has reversed the apostle's rule, and the congregation that measures its pastor's love by what he takes has been trained by the wrong men. Zechariah's burdensome stone is the other weight: Jerusalem set as a stone that every nation lifts and every lifter is torn by — the Lord's city, and the Lord's church, are heavier than the world that would carry them off.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek katanarkao (G2655), to be a dead weight, be burdensome; baros (G922), a weight; Hebrew ma'amasah (H4614), a burden, a heavy stone.

expand to see more

Greek katanarkao (G2655) — to burden, be a dead weight; 2 Corinthians 11:9, 12:13–14.

Greek en barei einai (G922) — to be burdensome, of weight; 1 Thessalonians 2:6.

Hebrew eben ma'amasah (H68, H4614) — a burdensome stone; Zechariah 12:3 only.

Usage

"“I will not be burdensome to you: for I seek not yours, but you” — the apostle's rule."

"“When we might have been burdensome, as the apostles of Christ” — a right set aside."

"“A burdensome stone for all people” — heavier than the nations that lift it."
